cards.question: What is a process, in the simplest definition?
cards.answer: An instance of an executing program.
distractors: A program stored on disk.
A single CPU instruction.
A thread inside the kernel.

cards.question: In the toy-shop analogy, what does a "process" correspond to?
cards.answer: An order of toys (has execution state, needs parts, and may need special hardware).
distractors: A worker in the toy shop.
The toy shop manager.
A workbench in the toy shop.

cards.question: What's the key difference between an "application" and a "process"?
cards.answer: An application is a static program on disk; a process is that program actively loaded and executing in memory.
distractors: An application runs in kernel mode; a process runs in user mode.
They're the same thing, just different names.
A process is stored on disk; an application is loaded in memory.

cards.question: Can one application produce multiple processes?
cards.answer: Yes — launching the same program twice creates two separate processes with independent state.
distractors: No — a program can only have one process at a time.
Yes — but all copies share the same state.
Only if the program is multithreaded.

cards.question: What OS abstraction encapsulates all of a process's state (code, data, variables)?
cards.answer: The address space.
distractors: The process control block.
The page table.
The stack.

cards.question: What are the 4 main regions of a process's address space?
cards.answer: Code/text, data, heap, stack.
distractors: Code, registers, cache, disk.
Heap, stack, PCB, page table.
Text, kernel, cache, swap.

cards.question: Which part of a process's address space holds static code and initial data?
cards.answer: The code/text and data regions (fixed at load time).
distractors: The heap.
The stack.
The page table.

cards.question: Which part of a process's address space holds dynamically allocated memory (e.g. malloc)?
cards.answer: The heap.
distractors: The stack.
The code/text region.
The PCB.

cards.question: Which part of a process's address space grows/shrinks in LIFO order to track function calls?
cards.answer: The stack.
distractors: The heap.
The data region.
The code/text region.

cards.question: Why is a stack's LIFO behavior useful during process execution?
cards.answer: It lets saved state be restored in the reverse order function calls were made (e.g. returning from a called procedure).
distractors: It lets any saved item be read in any order.
It keeps the heap from growing too large.
It lets the OS share the stack between processes.

cards.question: Why are the addresses in a process's address space called "virtual" addresses?
cards.answer: They don't have to correspond directly to actual physical memory locations.
distractors: They are only used by the kernel, never by processes.
They are stored on disk instead of memory.
They are fake addresses that are never actually accessed.

cards.question: What OS/hardware structure maps a process's virtual addresses to physical memory addresses?
cards.answer: The page table.
distractors: The process control block.
The ready queue.
The stack pointer.

cards.question: Why does decoupling virtual from physical addresses help the OS?
cards.answer: Physical memory management stays simple and independent of each process's data layout.
distractors: It makes every process use less memory.
It lets processes read each other's memory freely.
It removes the need for page tables.

cards.question: If two processes P1 and P2 run at the same time, can they use the exact same virtual address range?
cards.answer: Yes — the OS maps each process's identical virtual addresses to distinct physical memory locations.
distractors: No — the OS must give each process a different range.
No — only if they're the same program.
Yes — and they share the same physical memory.

cards.question: What 2 CPU register values define what a process is "doing" at a given moment?
cards.answer: The program counter (PC) and the stack pointer.
distractors: The heap pointer and the page table.
The process ID and the priority.
The cache and the TLB.

cards.question: What is a Process Control Block (PCB)?
cards.answer: A per-process data structure the OS maintains to track everything needed to manage/resume that process.
distractors: The CPU register that holds the current instruction.
A table mapping virtual to physical addresses.
A queue of processes waiting for the CPU.

cards.question: What are the main components stored in a PCB?
cards.answer: CPU state (PC, stack pointer, all registers) · memory mappings (virtual→physical translation) · list of open files · scheduling info (CPU time used, priority).
distractors: Only the program counter and the process ID.
The program's source code and compiler flags.
The cache contents and the TLB entries.

cards.question: When is a process's PCB created and initialized?
cards.answer: When the process is first created.
distractors: On every context switch.
The first time it touches the disk.
When the process terminates.

cards.question: Why doesn't the OS update the PCB's program-counter field on every single instruction?
cards.answer: The CPU tracks the current PC in a dedicated register while running; the OS only saves it to the PCB when the process stops running.
distractors: The PC never changes during execution.
The page table tracks the PC instead.
The PCB stores only the starting address of the program.

cards.question: What is a context switch?
cards.answer: The OS mechanism for switching CPU execution from one process's context to another's.
distractors: The switch from user mode to kernel mode on a syscall.
Copying a process's memory to disk.
Creating a child process with fork.

cards.question: What are the "direct costs" of a context switch?
cards.answer: CPU cycles spent saving/loading PCB register values to/from memory.
distractors: Cache misses after the new process starts.
Time spent waiting on disk I/O.
Time spent running the scheduling algorithm only.

cards.question: What are the "indirect costs" of a context switch?
cards.answer: Losing cache locality — the new process's data evicts the old process's data from the CPU cache.
distractors: Cycles spent saving and loading registers.
Rebuilding the page table on disk.
The time to fork a new process.

cards.question: What does it mean for a process's cache to be "hot"?
cards.answer: Most of its data is currently present in the CPU cache, so accesses are fast.
distractors: The CPU is physically overheating from use.
The cache is full and must be flushed.
The process has been running longer than its timeslice.

cards.question: Even with a hot cache, why might the OS still context switch away from a process?
cards.answer: A higher-priority process needs to run, or the process's timeslice has expired.
distractors: The hot cache might malfunction.
A hot cache always forces a context switch.
The OS must flush a hot cache regularly.

cards.question: What are the 5 states in the basic process life cycle?
cards.answer: New, ready, running, waiting, terminated.
distractors: Created, loaded, running, sleeping, killed.
Ready, running, blocked, swapped, zombie.
New, active, idle, waiting, finished.

cards.question: What happens in the "new" state of a process's life cycle?
cards.answer: The OS performs admission control and initializes the PCB and initial resources.
distractors: The process runs its first instruction.
The process waits for I/O to complete.
The scheduler dispatches it onto the CPU.

cards.question: What moves a process from "ready" to "running"?
cards.answer: The scheduler dispatches it onto the CPU.
distractors: Its I/O operation completes.
It calls fork().
It is admitted by admission control.

cards.question: What moves a running process back to "ready" (instead of "waiting")?
cards.answer: It's interrupted/preempted for a context switch (not waiting on I/O or an event).
distractors: It starts a disk read.
It calls exit().
Its I/O completes.

cards.question: What moves a running process into the "waiting" state?
cards.answer: It initiates a long operation (e.g. disk I/O) or waits on an event (timer, keyboard input).
distractors: Its timeslice expires.
The scheduler dispatches another process.
It is newly created.

cards.question: What moves a waiting process back to "ready"?
cards.answer: Its I/O operation completes or the event it was waiting on occurs.
distractors: The scheduler preempts it.
It calls exec().
Its timeslice expires.

cards.question: In which process states can the CPU actually run/dispatch the process?
cards.answer: Running and ready (ready processes are eligible; they just need the scheduler to dispatch them).
distractors: Running and waiting.
Only running.
New and ready.

cards.question: What two OS mechanisms does the P2L1 lecture name for process creation?
cards.answer: fork and exec (fork creates the new process; exec loads a new program into an existing one).
distractors: create and destroy (create makes the process; destroy removes it).
spawn and kill (spawn starts a process; kill ends it).
open and exec (open loads the program; exec runs it).

cards.question: What does fork() do?
cards.answer: Creates a new PCB for the child, copying the parent's PCB values — both continue executing right after the fork call.
distractors: Replaces the current program image with a new program.
Creates a new thread inside the same process.
Starts a new program from its first instruction with an empty PCB.

cards.question: What does exec() do?
cards.answer: Replaces a (forked) child's program image with a new program — its PC now points to the new program's first instruction.
distractors: Copies the parent's PCB into a new child process.
Creates a new thread that shares the address space.
Terminates the child and returns its exit code.

cards.question: On Unix-based systems, which process is the ancestor of all other processes?
cards.answer: init.
distractors: kernel.
shell.
systemd-login.

cards.question: On Android, which daemon process is the parent of all app processes?
cards.answer: Zygote.
distractors: init.
launchd.
Dalvik.

cards.question: What are the 3 main jobs of the CPU scheduler?
cards.answer: Preempt the running process, run the scheduling algorithm to pick the next one, dispatch it onto the CPU.
distractors: Allocate memory, map pages, evict pages.
Handle interrupts, service syscalls, schedule I/O.
Create processes, fork threads, join threads.

cards.question: Why must the CPU scheduler itself be efficient?
cards.answer: Time spent scheduling is time not spent running actual application processes.
distractors: The scheduler runs in user mode and can be preempted.
The scheduler must run on every instruction.
Slow schedulers cause cache corruption.

cards.question: In CPU-utilization terms, why does a longer timeslice (Tp) improve efficiency?
cards.answer: Scheduling overhead (Tsched) is fixed per switch, so a larger Tp:Tsched ratio means a higher fraction of time is spent on useful work.
distractors: A longer timeslice makes each context switch cheaper.
A longer timeslice reduces cache misses to zero.
A longer timeslice lets more processes run at once.

cards.question: Name the 4 ways a process can end up in the ready queue.
cards.answer: I/O completes; timeslice expires; process is newly forked; an awaited interrupt/event occurs.
distractors: A syscall starts; the cache is hot; the process calls exit; the heap grows.
The process calls join; memory is freed; a page is swapped out; a lock is released.
The scheduler preempts it; I/O starts; the process forks a child; a signal is sent.

cards.question: Does the CPU scheduler control when I/O operations or external events complete?
cards.answer: No — it has no control over those (only over timer-interrupt-driven context switches and the ready queue).
distractors: Yes — it schedules all I/O completions.
Yes — it decides when every interrupt fires.
Only for disk I/O, not network I/O.

cards.question: What is IPC (inter-process communication)?
cards.answer: OS mechanisms that let processes exchange data across address spaces while preserving isolation/protection.
distractors: A way for threads in one process to share variables.
The OS scheduling processes across CPUs.
Copying a process's memory to another machine.

cards.question: How does message-passing IPC work?
cards.answer: Processes write/send and read/receive messages through an OS-managed communication channel.
distractors: The OS maps one memory region into both processes.
Processes read each other's memory directly.
The processes share a single stack.

cards.question: What's the main benefit of message-passing IPC?
cards.answer: Uses standard OS-provided APIs/system calls, so it's simple and uniform.
distractors: No kernel involvement after setup.
No data is ever copied.
It needs no system calls at all.

cards.question: What's the main downside of message-passing IPC?
cards.answer: Overhead — every message is copied from sender's space → kernel channel → receiver's space.
distractors: Setting up the shared mapping is expensive.
No standard API, so it's error-prone.
Messages can only be one byte long.

cards.question: How does shared-memory IPC work?
cards.answer: The OS maps a shared memory region into both processes' address spaces; they read/write it directly.
distractors: Processes send messages through a kernel buffer.
The OS copies each write into the other process.
Each process gets a read-only copy of the other's memory.

cards.question: What's the main benefit of shared-memory IPC?
cards.answer: No OS involvement in the actual data path, so per-access overhead is very low.
distractors: It uses standard OS APIs, so it's simple.
The OS enforces synchronization automatically.
It needs no setup at all.

cards.question: What's the main downside of shared-memory IPC?
cards.answer: No fixed API — the OS is "out of the way," so usage is more error-prone and often needs custom synchronization code.
distractors: Every message is copied through the kernel.
It can only be used by threads, not processes.
It requires a network connection.

cards.question: Is shared-memory IPC always faster than message passing?
cards.answer: It depends — the setup/mapping cost is expensive, so it only pays off if amortized over enough messages.
distractors: Yes — shared memory never copies data.
No — shared memory is always slower.
Yes — the OS is never involved.

cards.question: What other terms mean the same as "process"?
cards.answer: Task or job.
distractors: Thread or fiber.
Program or binary.
Kernel or daemon.

cards.question: Is a waiting process still a process?
cards.answer: Yes. It's active state, even if not running on the CPU.
cards.memory: Process = executing *state*, not necessarily on the CPU.
distractors: No. It becomes a program again until it runs.
No. The OS deletes its PCB while it waits.
Only if it holds a lock.

cards.question: Can parts of a process's heap be unallocated ("holes")?
cards.answer: Yes. Parts may be unallocated, and the process can't access them.
cards.memory: Heap = Swiss cheese; touching a hole = segfault.
distractors: No. The heap is always one contiguous block.
No. Holes only occur in the stack.
Yes, and the process can read them freely.

cards.question: How big is a 32-bit virtual address space?
cards.answer: 4 GB (2^32 bytes)
distractors: 32 MB
4 TB
64 GB

cards.question: Where can parts of a process's address space live besides RAM?
cards.answer: Swapped out to disk.
distractors: In the CPU cache only.
In the PCB.
In another process's address space.

cards.question: Besides mapping virtual addresses to physical ones, what does the OS use a process's page table for?
cards.answer: Checking that each memory access is valid.
distractors: Choosing which process runs next.
Storing the process's open files.
Saving the CPU registers on a context switch.

cards.question: For each process, what memory information must the OS keep track of?
cards.answer: Its virtual → physical (or disk) mappings.
cards.memory: Every virtual address needs a "where is it really?" entry.
distractors: A copy of its entire memory on disk.
Its cache contents.
The source code of its program.

cards.question: Roughly how long does a CPU cache access take compared with a main-memory access?
cards.answer: Cache: a few cycles. Memory: hundreds of cycles.
cards.memory: Cache = desk drawer. Memory = the basement.
distractors: Cache: hundreds of cycles. Memory: a few cycles.
Both about one cycle.
Cache: a few cycles. Memory: millions of cycles.

cards.question: Does "hot cache" mean the cache is physically hot?
cards.answer: No. It means most accesses are cache hits.
distractors: Yes, and the OS must context switch to cool it.
It means the cache is full and must be flushed.
It means most accesses miss the cache.

cards.question: What does a process return when it terminates?
cards.answer: An exit code (success or error).
distractors: Its full memory image.
A new PCB for its parent.
Nothing; the OS just deletes it.

cards.question: Where does a new user's shell process come from?
cards.answer: It's created at login, and it spawns commands as children.
cards.memory: Process tree: init → login → shell → ls
distractors: It's created by the scheduler on boot.
It's the init process itself.
It's loaded from disk each time a command runs.

cards.question: What does the CPU scheduler decide besides who runs next?
cards.answer: How long the process may run (its timeslice).
distractors: Which pages to evict.
When I/O operations complete.
How much memory the process gets.

cards.question: Each process runs for a timeslice Tp, and the scheduler takes Tsched to run between processes. What is the CPU utilization?
cards.answer: 2Tp / (2Tp + 2Tsched), i.e., Tp / (Tp + Tsched).
distractors: Tsched / (Tp + Tsched).
Tp / Tsched.
Tp − Tsched.

cards.question: What is the CPU utilization when the timeslice Tp equals the scheduler's run time Tsched?
What is the CPU utilization when the timeslice Tp is 10 × the scheduler's run time Tsched?
cards.memory: A longer timeslice means less overhead.

cards.question: Where does a process wait during a disk read?
cards.answer: In the I/O queue for that device.
cards.memory: Each device has its own waiting line.
distractors: In the ready queue.
In the PCB of the disk.
On the CPU, spinning.

cards.question: After its I/O completes, where does a process go?
cards.answer: The ready queue (or straight to the CPU if nothing else is waiting).
distractors: Straight back to the I/O queue.
It is terminated.
It returns to the "new" state.

cards.question: Is maintaining the I/O queue the scheduler's job?
cards.answer: No. The scheduler maintains the ready queue.
cards.memory: The scheduler owns the ready line only.
distractors: Yes. The scheduler maintains all queues.
Yes. It decides when each I/O finishes.

cards.question: Can the CPU scheduler control when external events (like I/O completions) happen?
cards.answer: No, except for timer interrupts.
cards.memory: The scheduler controls the clock, not the disk.
distractors: Yes, it controls all interrupts.

cards.question: Give an example of a multi-process application.
cards.answer: A web server front end plus a database back end.
cards.memory: Web front end ↔ DB back end talk via IPC.
distractors: A single-threaded calculator.
